title: Targeted search: finding the clients that fit your service for Pet grooming
audience: Groomers, including mobile groomers, who want more work from businesses in their area, and who want to contact them lawfully.
learningOutcomes: Build a prospect list that is scored against written fit criteria for service area, job size and repeat need.
Identify public signals that a client need is starting, and explain why each one is a reasonable reason to make contact.
Write a first approach that makes one specific, verifiable observation, offers one small next step and can be declined easily.

instruction.heading: Decide the grooms you want before you look for them
instruction.body: Targeted search starts with a clear picture of the work you want. Write down the services you do well (a bath, a full clip, de-shedding), the price you can sustain, the postcodes you can reach without losing money on travel, and how often each client needs a groom. A recurring booking on a route you already run is worth far more to a small business than a single groom across town. These criteria are the filter for everything that follows.

instruction.heading: Score prospects against the criteria
instruction.body: Keep every prospect in one list with a fit column and a status column. Score each as strong fit, possible fit or not a fit. Ask whether the prospect sits inside your service area, has a repeat need, has a person who makes the buying decision, and needs work your registration, licence and insurance cover. Businesses that keep dogs on site, such as daycare or boarding businesses, and pet-friendly offices are examples to evaluate, but add a prospect only when it passes the criteria. Record the date each entry was added and where its details came from, and use only contact details published for business use. Do not buy or harvest lists: ACMA's guidance says buying a list does not remove the need to show consent (ACMA, 28 March 2019; an older source).

instruction.heading: Watch for signals that a need is starting
instruction.body: A signal is a public event that makes a need more likely soon. Examples include a public notice of planned building works, a new business opening on a street you already serve, a change of occupier at a site you already serve, or a competitor closing in your area. Use signals to decide when to contact a business, not to build a profile of people. Do not monitor private people or go to a home to make an offer. Buying for Victoria lists current and past tenders and lets suppliers set alerts (Victorian Government, 7 August 2026). Check your own council's planning register where one is published.

instruction.heading: Make a first approach that is specific and easy to decline
instruction.body: A useful first message says how you came to know about the business, makes one observation you can verify from public view or from the business's own published material, and offers one small next step, such as a fifteen-minute call or a written price for one animal on stated terms. Keep it short, do not overstate what you know, and make it simple to say no. The ACCC's 2026 review of unsolicited selling found that many approaches were pressured or misleading (ACCC, 28 July 2026), so an honest, specific message is also a practical advantage.

instruction.heading: Follow up on a fixed schedule and stop when asked
instruction.body: Decide in advance how many follow-ups you will send and how far apart. Stop when someone says no or asks you to stop: remove them at once and record the date. At the end of each month, review which fit tier and which signal produced paid work.

procedure: Write the services, area, price and repeat-need criteria for the work you want.
Build the prospect list and score each entry as strong fit, possible fit or not a fit, with a reason and a contact source.
Choose two or three public signals to watch and note the date each one is seen.
Write one first message for each fit tier, with the source of the contact, one verifiable observation and one small next step.
Check each message against the electronic message rules, and against your registration, licence and insurance, before sending.
Send to strong-fit prospects first, follow up on the fixed schedule, and remove anyone who asks you to stop.

workedExamples.situation: A mobile groomer covers three suburbs. A daycare business in one of them posts a public notice about planned works at its premises, and its general office email address is published on its website. The groomer has no existing link to the business.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Should she send a sales email now, and what should it contain?
workedExamples.reasoning: She should not send a sales email just because the address is published. ACMA's Spam Act guidance says that publishing an address does not by itself permit commercial messages (ACMA, last updated 28 March 2019; an older source). She checks whether the business has agreed to receive marketing or has invited contact, and if not, she waits for an invitation or uses a route the business has agreed to. A call to a registered number is limited by the Do Not Call Register, so she checks the register first. Any message names the notice, says how she learned of it, offers one specific item she could handle, and asks one question. She offers only the services her registration and insurance cover, and she does not offer a mobile grooming service in Victoria until she has checked the Victorian position with the council, which the research did not settle.

equipmentAndPpe: Prospect list in a spreadsheet or notebook, with fit and status columns
Written fit criteria for service area, service type and repeat need
Message templates checked against the electronic message rules
No PPE is needed for desk work; any site visit follows the site's own safety rules

commonErrors.error: Sending the same message to everyone on a broad list
commonErrors.prevention: Score the list first, write one message for each fit tier, and start with the strong-fit tier.

commonErrors.error: Using private information about an individual to make contact
commonErrors.prevention: Use only contact details published for business use, or details the person gave you for this purpose.

commonErrors.error: Pitching a service you are not registered, licensed or insured to deliver
commonErrors.prevention: Check your registration, licence and insurance before outreach, and remove that service from the message.

commonErrors.error: Following up without a limit, or continuing after a request to stop
commonErrors.prevention: Set a fixed number of follow-ups and a stop rule, and record every stop request.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Do not offer a licensed or registered service in outreach unless you hold the authority that the state or territory where the work is done requires. This lesson does not grant any licence, registration or authority. Rules differ between states and territories, and Victorian grooming rules are UNRESOLVED.

Commercial electronic messages, including email and text, are regulated by the Spam Act 2003 (Cth). ACMA says marketing messages need consent, that consent should be recorded, and that unsubscribe requests must be honoured within five working days. The Spam Act text was not read for this research, so check it before sending.

Information on a public listing or a public notice does not by itself permit contact about anything. If the Privacy Act applies to your business, OAIC guidance says public information is not exempt from the direct-marketing rules. Use only contact details published for business use, keep them secure, and stop when someone objects.

qualityStandard: Every prospect on the list has a fit score, a reason for that score and a recorded source for its contact details.
Every first message contains one verifiable observation and one small, easy-to-decline next step.
No contact is made using private information, and every stop request is recorded and actioned.
documentationEvidence: Prospect list with fit score, reason, status, source and date added
Signal log with the date each public signal was seen
Stop-request record with the date it was actioned
summary: Define the grooms you want first, then filter prospects against that definition.
Watch public signals, and never use private information to make contact.
Keep the first approach specific and easy to decline, and stop when asked.

knowledgeChecks.question: Which prospect should a groomer contact first?
options: A one-off job well outside your service area, because it looks large
A business with several sites inside your service area that you already visit
Any business that has a website, because it probably spends money on services

knowledgeChecks.question: A public notice shows planned works at a business on your route. What is the most appropriate first step?
options: Contact the business by a route that the electronic message and do-not-call rules allow
Message each employee using their private contact details
Go onto the site to look at the work before making contact

knowledgeChecks.question: Before you send a commercial email to a prospect, what should you do?
options: Check that the message is short enough to read on a phone and has a fun subject line
Ask the prospect to like your social media page first
Confirm the Spam Act 2003 requirements in current ACMA guidance before sending
